title: Solar Water Purification
summary: Eliminate pathogens using sunlight. No chemicals, no electricity, no filters.
steps: Fill clear PET bottles 3/4 full with potentially contaminated water.
Shake vigorously for 30 seconds to oxygenate the water.
Fill the rest of the bottle, leaving minimal air gap.
Place bottles on a reflective surface (corrugated metal, aluminum foil) in direct sunlight.
Expose for 6 hours in clear weather, or 2 consecutive days if cloudy.
Water is safe to drink once the UV-A radiation has destroyed pathogen DNA.
Store treated water in the same bottle, in a cool dark place, for up to 6 months.
notes: SODIS (Solar Water Disinfection) method. Validated by WHO and extensively tested in developing countries. Effective against bacteria, viruses, and protozoa. Does NOT remove chemical contaminants or heavy metals.

title: Water Boiling Protocol
summary: The oldest and most reliable water purification method. Works everywhere.
steps: Filter cloudy water through cloth first to remove particulates.
Bring water to a rolling boil (large bubbles continuously breaking the surface).
Maintain rolling boil for at least 1 minute (3 minutes at altitudes above 2000m).
Let cool naturally. Do not add cold water to speed cooling.
Store in clean, covered containers.
Taste improvement: pour between containers 3-4 times to re-oxygenate.
notes: 100% effective against all biological pathogens. Does not remove chemical contamination. Fuel requirements may be significant in resource-scarce environments.

title: Solar Food Drying
summary: Preserve fruits, vegetables, and meat using only sun and airflow.
steps: Build a simple box dryer: dark-bottomed box with screen shelves and clear top cover.
Cut food into thin, uniform slices (3-6mm for fruits, 5mm for meat).
Arrange food on screens in a single layer, no overlapping.
Place dryer in direct sunlight, elevated to allow airflow underneath.
Ensure temperature reaches 50-60°C inside the dryer.
Turn food daily. Drying time: 1-2 days for fruits/vegetables, 2-3 days for meat.
Properly dried food should be leathery, not sticky. No moisture spots.
Store in airtight containers in a cool, dark place. Shelf life: 6-12 months.
notes: Reduces food waste from 30-50% to near zero in agricultural communities. Preserves most nutritional value. Critical for food security in tropical regions with seasonal abundance.

title: Emergency Caloric Garden (30-Day Yield)
summary: Rapid-yield crops that produce food within 30 days. No experience required.
steps: Select fast-growing crops: radishes (25 days), spinach/lettuce (30 days), bush beans (45 days).
Prepare soil: loosen to 15cm depth, remove rocks and weeds. Mix with compost if available.
Plant radish seeds 2cm deep, 5cm apart. Plant greens broadcast-style, thin later.
Water daily (morning or evening) keeping soil moist but not waterlogged.
Thin seedlings to prevent overcrowding when 5cm tall.
Harvest radishes at 25 days. Harvest outer leaves of greens continuously from day 30.
Replant immediately after harvesting to maintain continuous yield.
notes: 10m² can produce 2-4kg of fresh food per month after initial 30 days. Complement with longer-season crops (potatoes, squash) planted simultaneously for month 2+ yield.

title: Bicycle Generator (12V)
summary: Generate electricity with a bicycle, a car alternator, and a battery.
steps: Mount the bicycle securely with the rear wheel elevated.
Attach the alternator to the bicycle frame, aligned with the rear wheel via belt drive.
Connect alternator to the voltage regulator.
Connect voltage regulator to the 12V battery (respect + / - polarity).
Pedal at moderate speed (60-80 RPM) to begin charging.
1 hour of pedaling produces approximately 100-150 Watt-hours.
Sufficient to charge phones (5Wh each), LED lights, and small radios.
Use an inverter for AC devices, but efficiency drops — stick to DC where possible.
notes: Human power output: 75-150W sustained. Not viable for heating or heavy loads. Ideal for communications (radios, phones, mesh network nodes) in off-grid or crisis scenarios.

title: Micro Solar Setup (50W)
summary: Minimum viable solar power for communications and lighting.
steps: Mount solar panel facing the equator, tilted at your latitude angle.
Connect panel to charge controller (panel + and - to controller solar inputs).
Connect battery to charge controller (battery + and - to controller battery outputs).
Connect USB converter to the load output of the charge controller.
Test voltage: panel should show 18-22V open circuit, battery 12-13V.
50W panel produces ~250Wh/day in good conditions.
Powers: 10W LED light (25 hours), phone charging (50+ charges), small radio (100+ hours).
Never connect the panel directly to the battery — always use a charge controller.
notes: Cost: $40-80 total for basic components. A 50W system sustains a family's communications and lighting needs indefinitely in sunny climates. The single most impactful off-grid investment.

title: Mesh Network (LoRa/Meshtastic)
summary: Build an off-grid encrypted text messaging network using LoRa radios.
requirements: 2+ LoRa32 or LilyGO T-Beam devices ($30 each)
Line of sight between nodes (up to 10km)
steps: Flash Meshtastic firmware on each LoRa device (via web flasher at flasher.meshtastic.org).
Configure each node: set unique name, set frequency (868MHz EU / 915MHz US), enable encryption.
Connect node to phone via Bluetooth. Open Meshtastic app.
Set encryption key — share the same key with all trusted nodes.
Position nodes as high as possible (roof, tower, tree). Range depends on line of sight.
Messages hop automatically between nodes. A 4-node mesh can cover an entire city.
Each node can also relay GPS positions, enabling location tracking without internet.
Battery: a 18650 cell powers a node for 2-3 days. Solar panel extends indefinitely.
notes: Meshtastic is open-source, AES-256 encrypted, requires no cellular or internet. Ideal for coordinating during protests, natural disasters, or communications blackouts. [STUB: production deployment requires coordinated frequency planning]

title: Digital Dead Drop Protocol
summary: Exchange information at a predetermined location without direct contact.
requirements: Password-protected USB drive or microSD card
steps: Agree on 3-5 dead drop locations in advance. Choose inconspicuous spots.
Create a Veracrypt encrypted volume on the USB drive. Use a strong passphrase.
Compose message as a plain text file inside the encrypted volume.
Physically deposit the drive at the agreed location.
Signal completion via an innocuous public signal (specific hashtag, classified ad, chalk mark).
Recipient retrieves drive within a pre-agreed window (e.g., 48 hours).
Recipient mounts volume, reads/copies message, optionally replaces with response.
Sanitize: wipe metadata from all files. Never connect an unknown USB to your primary device.
notes: This protocol predates the internet. Used by intelligence agencies, resistance movements, and dissidents worldwide. The digital version adds encryption. [See also: V for X → A Teia branch for digital dead drops]

title: Field First Aid (No Supplies)
summary: Essential first aid techniques that require no medical supplies.
steps: SEVERE BLEEDING: Apply direct pressure with any clean cloth. Press hard. Do NOT remove a blood-soaked cloth — add more on top. Elevate the wound above heart level if possible.
CLEAN WATER SHORTAGE: Use the cleanest water available. Solar purification (see blueprint) is preferable to drinking contaminated water.
FRACTURE: Immobilize the limb using sticks, rolled magazines, or any rigid material. Pad with cloth. Secure with strips of fabric. Do NOT attempt to reset the bone.
BURNS: Cool immediately with running water for 20 minutes. Do NOT apply butter, oil, or ice. Cover with clean cloth. Leave blisters intact.
HYPOTHERMIA: Remove wet clothing. Share body heat. Warm drinks if conscious. Warm core first (torso, not extremities).
HEAT STROKE: Move to shade. Cool with water on skin. Fan continuously. Do NOT give fluids if unconscious.
CHOKING: 5 back blows between shoulder blades, then 5 abdominal thrusts (Heimlich). Repeat as needed.
notes: These techniques save lives with zero equipment. Memorize them. Practice them. When infrastructure fails, knowledge is the only tool that cannot be confiscated.

title: Digital OpSec Basics
summary: Core operational security practices for digital activity under surveillance.
steps: DEVICE ISOLATION: Never use your primary device for sensitive activity. Use a dedicated device if possible.
METADATA: Every photo contains GPS coordinates. Every document contains author info. Strip metadata before sharing any file.
COMMUNICATIONS: Signal for encrypted messaging. Tor Browser for anonymous web access. Never use work or government devices.
BROWSER HYGIENE: Use Tor Browser or a hardened Firefox (Privacy Badger, uBlock Origin, NoScript). Clear cookies on close.
PASSWORDS: Use a password manager (KeePassXC, Bitwarden). Unique password for each service. Never reuse.
TWO FACTOR: Enable 2FA on all accounts. Prefer authenticator apps over SMS. Hardware key (YubiKey) if available.
SOCIAL MEDIA: Assume everything you post is permanent and public. No real names, no real photos, no location data.
PATTERN DISRUPTION: Vary your routine. Don't access sensitive services at predictable times from predictable locations.
notes: See also: V for X → The Mask branch for comprehensive OpSec guide and identity protection tools.

title: Mutual Aid Network Setup
summary: Build a community self-help network from scratch. No technology required.
steps: CORE GROUP: Start with 3-5 trusted people. Agree on principles: solidarity, not charity. No hierarchy. Everyone contributes what they can.
NEEDS INVENTORY: Survey what people need (food, child care, transport, skills). Survey what people can offer. Match them.
REGULAR CONTACT: Weekly meeting. In person. Keep minutes in a shared notebook. No digital footprint.
RESOURCE POOL: Create a shared fund (cash, not bank). Track contributions and distributions transparently.
COMMUNICATION TREE: Each person contacts 3 others. Cascade system for rapid information sharing without group chats.
SKILL SHARES: Weekly knowledge exchange. Someone teaches water purification, another teaches first aid. Knowledge is the most resilient resource.
EXPANSION: Each member recruits 1-2 new people per month. Growth should be organic and trust-based.
SECURITY: No membership lists. No photos. No social media. The network's strength is in its invisibility.
notes: Mutual aid networks are how communities survive crises when institutions fail. Historical success: Black Panther Free Breakfast Program, Argentine horizontalidad, Puerto Rico mutual post-Maria.

title: Nonviolent Resistance Strategy
summary: Data shows nonviolent campaigns succeed 53% of the time vs 26% for armed insurgency.
requirements: Mass participation (3.5% of population for near-certain success)
steps: CHENOWETH DATA: Nonviolent campaigns succeed 53% of the time. Armed campaigns succeed 26%. Mass nonviolent participation is the single strongest predictor of success.
PARTICIPATION THRESHOLD: Research shows that when 3.5% of a population participates in sustained nonviolent action, no campaign has failed.
PILLARS OF SUPPORT: Identify which institutions sustain the opponent (military, police, bureaucracy, media, economic elites). Target these for defection, not destruction.
TACTICS DIVERSITY: Use over 198 documented methods (Sharp's 198 Methods of Nonviolent Action). Variety prevents adaptation.
BACKFIRE: Opponent violence against nonviolent protesters causes political jiu-jitsu — it strengthens the movement and weakens the opponent.
DISCIPLINE: Maintain strict nonviolent discipline even under provocation. Any violence by protesters destroys the backfire effect.
COORDINATION: Maintain communication. See: V for X → A Teia (anonymous comms) and Protocol X → Mesh Network.
SUSTAINABILITY: Plan for the long term. Build mutual aid (see blueprint) to sustain participants during prolonged campaigns.
notes: Source: Erica Chenoweth, 'Why Civil Resistance Works' (2011). Analysis of 323 campaigns 1900-2006. Nonviolent campaigns are also more likely to lead to democratic, peaceful societies post-conflict.
